title: Chapter 2: I can do this
subtitle: Thermal energy and electromagnetic radiation

sections.name: Thermal energy, electromagnetic radiation and global warming

prac_text: Prac done and written up in my log book

rows.text: Describe thermal energy as the sum of the random kinetic energy and potential energy of the atoms and molecules of an object or system
rows.question: Which of the following statements about thermal energy is correct?
options: The thermal energy of an object can be increased by increasing its thermal conductivity.
Increasing the total potential energy of an object’s molecules increases its thermal energy.
Increasing the heat capacity of an object will increase its thermal energy.
Changing the temperature of an object is unlikely to change its thermal energy.

rows.text: Understand that increases and decreases of temperature are related to increases and decreases of thermal energy in a system
rows.question: Which of the following changes will increase the temperature of an object?
options: increasing its heat capacity
increasing the random kinetic energy of its molecules
decreasing its thermal conductivity
converting the potential energy of some of its molecules to random kinetic energy

rows.text: Convert temperatures between Celsius and kelvin
rows.question: Which is a lower temperature: –200°C or 63 K?

rows.text: Analyse qualitatively thermal energy transfers in terms of conduction, convection, radiation and evaporation using a particle model
rows.question: A silver spoon is placed in a hot cup of tea. After a short time, the handle of the spoon becomes much warmer. Describe the mechanism by which thermal energy is transferred along the spoon.
rows.answer: Conduction along the metal, mainly through interactions (collisions) of the loose electrons, which pass energy from particle to particle.

rows.question: Which of the following is the best definition of the specific heat capacity of an object?
options: the energy required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K
the energy required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K in 1 s
the energy per kg required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K in 1 s
the energy per kg required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K

rows.text: Define specific latent heats of vaporisation (condensation) and fusion (melting), $L$
rows.question: Which of the following is the best definition of the specific latent heat of fusion?
options: the energy required to melt 1 kg of the material involved in 1 s
the energy required to melt 1 kg of the material involved
the energy required to raise the temperature enough to melt 1 kg of the material involved
the energy required to raise the temperature enough to melt 1 kg of the material involved in 1 s

rows.text: Carry out practical investigations involving changing the temperature or state of a substance
rows.prac: Practical 2A-2: Specific heat capacity of water

rows.text: Analyse quantitatively the thermal energy changes associated with temperature and state changes
rows.question: A 250 W immersion heater is used to bring 0.50 kg of water at 20°C to the boil. The specific heat capacity of water is 4190 J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. Ignoring thermal energy losses, and the energy to heat the heater itself, the time that this would take is closest to
options: 11 minutes.
14 minutes.
22 minutes.
28 minutes.

rows.text: Use the equation $Q = mc\Delta T$ to calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of a substance
rows.stem: Students observe a dish of ice melting in the sunlight. There is 250 g of ice; it is initially at 0°C. They stop the observation when all the ice has turned to water at 15°C.
rows.question: How much energy is required to raise the 250 g of water at 0°C to 15°C?

rows.text: Use the equation $Q = mL$ to calculate the energy needed to change the state of a substance
rows.stem: Students observe a dish of ice melting in the sunlight. There is 250 g of ice; it is initially at 0°C. They stop the observation when all the ice has turned to water at 15°C.
rows.question: How much energy in kJ is required to convert the ice at 0°C to water at 0°C?

rows.text: Describe the general features of a blackbody object
rows.question: A blackbody is an object that
options: is painted with black paint.
is only visible when black light shines on it
does not reflect any frequencies of electromagnetic radiation
only emits certain electromagnetic radiation frequencies

rows.text: Use Wien’s law ($\lambda_{max}T = 2.90 \times 10^{-3}$ m K) to calculate the peak emitting wavelengths of objects modelled as blackbodies
rows.question:
A temperature sensor measures the forehead of a person’s temperature to be 36.6°C.
Use Wien’s law to estimate which of the following wavelengths is closest to the peak wavelength.
options: 9.4 μm
9.7 μm
11 μm
79 μm

rows.text: Use graphical methods to compare total energy radiated by objects modelled as blackbodies
rows.question: Which of the five graphs has the greatest total energy emission?
rows.answer: A. The 5500 K curve has the largest area under it.

rows.text: Identify the way concepts of thermal energy and electromagnetic radiation can help understanding of global warming and climate change
rows.question: The surface of Earth radiates about 400 W m$^{-2}$ of infrared radiation. Which of the following best describes what happens to this radiation?
options: About 10% of this radiation is absorbed by greenhouse gases; the rest escapes into space.
About 10% of this radiation escapes into space; the rest is converted into visible wavelengths.
About 10% of this radiation escapes into space; the rest is absorbed by the atmosphere.
Almost all of this radiation is reflected back to the surface.
